moments.title: What the video will cover
moments.text: The presenter introduces functions, input and output variables, notation and types of model.

moments.title: Input and output
moments.text: A function relates an allowed input to an output; the independent variable supplies the input.

moments.title: A child's height over time
moments.text: The example assumes a child is 50 cm at birth and 200 cm at age 15 to build a simple model.

moments.title: Choose variables and axes
moments.text: Age is the input and height is the output. The function notation $H(a)$ represents height at age $a$.

moments.title: A linear model
moments.text: The presenter sketches a straight-line model from 50 cm at birth to 200 cm at age 15 and notes that real growth may not be linear.

moments.title: Form the function
moments.text: The assumed rate is 150 cm over 15 years, or 10 cm per year, giving $H(a)=10a+50$.

moments.title: Evaluate a function
moments.text: Substituting $a=10$ gives $H(10)=150$ cm in the model.

moments.title: Types of functions
moments.text: The presenter briefly surveys linear, quadratic, exponential, logarithmic, sinusoidal and logistic models.

moments.title: A piecewise model
moments.text: To represent a change after age 15, the presenter suggests joining a linear growth rule to a constant-height rule.

notes.title: Function and model
notes.text: The child-height line is an illustrative assumption. The presenter notes that real growth can vary.
notes.write: A function assigns exactly one output to each allowed input. A model should be interpreted only over a suitable domain.

moments.title: Three ways to write a function
moments.text: $f(x)=x^2-2$, $f: x\mapsto x^2-2$ and $y=x^2-2$ all describe the same rule. Use whichever your textbook uses.

moments.title: Evaluate by substitution
moments.text: $f(3)=7$, $g(-2)=1$ and $h(24)=5$. Find the function, then substitute the input for $x$.

moments.title: Domain and range
moments.text: The domain is the set of possible inputs ($x$ values). The range is the set of possible outputs ($y$ values).

moments.title: Domain and range of a quadratic
moments.text: $f(x)=x^2-2$ goes left and right forever, so $x\in\mathbb{R}$. It bottoms out at $-2$, so $y\ge-2$.

moments.title: A straight line
moments.text: $g(x)=x+3$ goes on forever in every direction, so both domain and range are all real numbers.

moments.title: A square root function
moments.text: $h(x)=\sqrt{x+1}$ starts at $x=-1$ and only gives non-negative outputs: domain $x\ge-1$, range $y\ge0$.

moments.title: A composite is a function of a function
moments.text: In $f\circ g$, the output of $g$ becomes the input of $f$.

moments.title: Find $f\circ g$
moments.text: Write $f$, and where it has $x$, put in $g(x)=x+3$. The result is $(x+3)^2-2$.

moments.title: Find $g\circ f$
moments.text: Start with $g$ and put $f(x)$ where $x$ was: $x^2-2+3=x^2+1$. A different order gives a different function.

moments.title: Inverse functions and their notation
moments.text: The inverse of $f$ is written $f^{-1}$. Start from $y=f(x)$.

moments.title: Swap $x$ and $y$, then solve for $y$
moments.text: The first step is always to swap $x$ and $y$. Then use algebra to make $y$ the subject.

moments.title: The inverse of $h$
moments.text: From $y=\sqrt{x+1}$: swap, square both sides, subtract 1. $h^{-1}(x)=x^2-1$.

moments.title: The inverse is a reflection
moments.text: The graph of $f^{-1}$ is the graph of $f$ reflected in the line $y=x$.

notes.title: Restricting the quadratic domain
notes.text: The video finds a square-root inverse for $f(x)=x^2-2$ without first restricting the original domain. On all real numbers the function is not one-to-one.
notes.write: Restrict to $x\ge0$ to obtain $f^{-1}(x)=\sqrt{x+2}$ with domain $x\ge-2$; choosing $x\le0$ gives the negative branch.

notes.title: Domain of an inverse
notes.text: The video finds an inverse for $h(x)=\sqrt{x+1}$ but does not explicitly state its domain.
notes.write: The original range is $[0,\infty)$, so $h^{-1}(x)=x^2-1$ has domain $x\ge0$.

ican.text: I can explain what it means for a relation to be a function and use function notation.
I can evaluate a function and interpret input and output in context.
I can find a function's domain and range using algebra, a graph or stated restrictions.
I can explain when an inverse function exists and interpret it as reversing the original function.
I can relate the graph and domain of an inverse to the graph and range of the original function.
I can select a reasonable domain for a mathematical model and explain limitations.

ku.text: A function assigns exactly one output to each input in its stated domain. Different inputs may share an output; that does not prevent the relation from being a function.
The domain is the set of allowed inputs. The range is the set of outputs actually produced by those inputs, which may be narrower than the function's codomain.
When finding a real-valued domain, check restrictions such as a nonzero denominator and a nonnegative square-root radicand, then apply any restriction stated by the question or context.
$f^{-1}$ reverses $f$ when $f$ is one-to-one on its domain. A function that is not one-to-one may become invertible after an appropriate domain restriction.
The domain of $f^{-1}$ is the range of $f$, and its range is the domain of $f$. Their graphs are reflections in $y=x$ when the axes have the same scale.
Solving $f(x)=b$ asks for an input that produces $b$; where the inverse exists and $b$ lies in its domain, this input is $f^{-1}(b)$.
For a model, use the context to restrict inputs and interpret outputs. A formula can produce numbers outside the range where its assumptions are reasonable.

misc.weak: If two inputs have the same output, the relation is not a function.
misc.better: A function can map different inputs to the same output. It fails to be a function if one allowed input has more than one output.

misc.weak: The domain of $\sqrt{10-2x}$ is all real numbers.
The range of a function is always the set of all real numbers.
misc.better: The range consists only of outputs actually produced on the stated domain. For $\sqrt{10-2x}$ it is $[0,\infty)$.
$f^{-1}$ denotes the inverse function; $1/f(x)$ is a reciprocal where defined.

misc.weak: $f(x)=x^2-2$ has inverse $\sqrt{x+2}$ on all real inputs.
misc.better: The original function is not one-to-one on $\mathbb R$. Restrict its domain, for example to $x\ge0$, before using that inverse branch.

misc.weak: The inverse has the same domain as the original function.
misc.better: The inverse domain is the original range, and the inverse range is the original domain.

terms.text: Replace the input variable with the stated value, then calculate the output.
Identify all permitted inputs using algebraic and contextual restrictions; include or exclude endpoints correctly.
Determine all outputs produced on the stated domain and express them clearly.
Check one-to-one behaviour, exchange input and output, and give the relevant domain and interpretation.

worked.prompt: Consider the real-valued function $f(x)=\sqrt{10-2x}$ on its largest real domain.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Find the domain and range of $f$.
parts.a: Require $10-2x\ge0$, so the domain is $x\le5$. The square root is nonnegative and can grow without bound, so the range is $f(x)\ge0$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Solve $f(x)=4$ and explain what the result means.
parts.a: $\sqrt{10-2x}=4$ gives $10-2x=16$, so $x=-3$. The input $-3$ produces the output 4; substitution verifies it.

parts.label: (d)
parts.a: Swap $x$ and $y$ in $y=\sqrt{10-2x}$ and solve: $f^{-1}(x)=(10-x^2)/2$. Its domain is $x\ge0$, the original range.

kq.q: Why is $x^2$ a function but not one-to-one on all real numbers?
kq.model: Every input has one output, so it is a function. However, $2$ and $-2$ both produce 4, so it is not one-to-one on $\mathbb R$.

kq.q: Why must the inverse of a square-root function have a restricted domain?
kq.model: Its inputs are outputs of the original square-root function, and those outputs are nonnegative.

kq.q: Why can a function's algebraic domain differ from its modelling domain?
kq.model: The formula may be mathematically defined for inputs that do not make sense in the real situation, such as negative age.

kq.q: What does the graph reflection in $y=x$ tell us about an inverse?
kq.model: Each point $(a,b)$ on the original graph becomes $(b,a)$ on the inverse graph: inputs and outputs are exchanged.
